message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
2026 Employee Engagement Survey: Results Report
People Analytics Team, Brightwell Housing Association, April 2026

1. Summary
The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded. The overall engagement index rose from 65 to 68, its highest level since the survey began in 2019. This report sets out results by division and theme and recommends priorities for 2026-27.

2. Method
All 1,980 employees on the payroll on 1 March were invited by email, with paper questionnaires and protected time offered to repairs operatives without regular computer access. The survey was administered by an external provider and was confidential: no results are reported for groups of fewer than ten respondents. The engagement index is the mean of six questions on pride, advocacy, intention to stay, motivation, discretionary effort and satisfaction, scaled to 0-100. The questions are unchanged from 2025, so year-on-year comparisons are like for like.

3. Response and engagement by division
Table 1. Response rates and engagement index by division
Division | Headcount 2026 | Responses 2026 | Response rate 2026 | Response rate 2025 | Engagement 2025 | Engagement 2026
Repairs and Maintenance | 820 | 254 | 31% | 64% | 58 | 63
Housing Management | 610 | 427 | 70% | 78% | 69 | 70
Customer Services | 340 | 228 | 67% | 74% | 66 | 68
Central Services | 210 | 141 | 67% | 81% | 72 | 71
Total | 1,980 | 1,050 | 53% | 72% | 65 | 68

The overall response rate fell from 72% to 53%, which remains above the 50% benchmark our provider regards as robust for organisations of our size.

Every division improved its engagement score this year. The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63. Repairs has historically been our least engaged division, and in 2025 it was the focus of a major programme: new vans and tablets for all operatives, a revised bonus scheme and monthly team briefings led by the Director of Property. The results suggest this investment is paying off.

4. Results by theme
Table 2. Theme scores (percentage agreeing), organisation-wide
Theme | 2025 | 2026 | Change
My manager supports my development | 61% | 66% | +5
I have the tools to do my job well | 54% | 62% | +8
I understand the organisation's priorities | 70% | 72% | +2
Workload is manageable | 49% | 47% | -2
I would recommend Brightwell as a place to work | 58% | 63% | +5

Tools and equipment showed the biggest improvement of any theme, consistent with the investment in Repairs. Workload remains the weakest area and is the only theme to decline. Free-text comments on workload most often referred to vacancy cover in Housing Management, where 41 posts were vacant at the time of the survey.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Extend the Repairs model of regular director-led briefings to Housing Management and Customer Services in 2026-27, given the improvement it has delivered in Repairs.
5.2 Prioritise recruitment to Housing Management vacancies, with a target to halve the vacancy count by October.
5.3 Repeat the survey in March 2027 with the same questions and method.

6. Conclusion
2026 shows real and broad-based progress. Engagement is at its highest level since 2019, every division improved, and the division where we invested most improved most. The Executive Team can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked, and should extend its most effective elements across the organisation.
</document>
response:
# Review: 2026 Employee Engagement Survey Results Report

The report is clear and well organised, but it has two factual errors, and its main conclusion rests on evidence that the data doesn't support. It needs revision before going to the Executive Team.

## 1. Factual errors

**Respondent count is inconsistent.** Section 1 says 1,150 colleagues responded. Table 1 shows 1,050, and 1,050 / 1,980 gives the reported 53%. The figure in Section 1 should be 1,050.

**"Every division improved" is false.** Central Services fell from 72 to 71. The claim appears twice (Section 3 and the Conclusion) and also supports the "broad-based progress" framing. A one-point fall is probably noise, but the statement as written is wrong.

## 2. The Repairs result is unreliable

The Repairs response rate halved, from 64% to 31%. Only 254 of 820 operatives responded, against about 525 last year. The report doesn't mention this, and the 50% benchmark is applied only to the overall rate, which hides the problem.

With a drop this large, the 2026 Repairs respondents may be a different group from 2025's. Less engaged staff are typically less likely to respond, so the five-point gain could come partly or entirely from who answered rather than a real change. Nothing in the report lets a reader tell these apart.

The drop is also surprising given the support offered: tablets, paper questionnaires and protected time. It needs explaining. Possible causes include a change in how paper forms were distributed, the timing relative to workload, or survey fatigue or distrust.

**Suggested additions:**
- A response-rate breakdown within Repairs (by trade, area or team) and a check of the respondents' profile against 2025.
- A comparison of tablet versus paper response routes in both years.
- A clear caveat that the Repairs change cannot be confirmed as genuine.

## 3. The organisation-wide rise is partly about who responded

Repairs, the lowest-scoring division, fell from about 37% of respondents in 2025 to 24% in 2026. A smaller share of low scorers raises the overall average even if nobody's views changed.

My rough check, assuming 2025 headcounts were similar to 2026:

| Basis | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Respondent-weighted (as reported) | ~65 | ~68 |
| Weighted by headcount | ~64 | ~67 |

The headcount-weighted rise still includes the uncertain Repairs gain. The "highest since 2019" headline should therefore be caveated. The report should also state how the overall index is calculated and consider reporting a headcount-weighted figure.

The same issue affects Table 2. The +8 rise in "I have the tools to do my job well" is presented as consistent with the Repairs investment. Yet Repairs makes up a smaller share of respondents, and no divisional breakdown is shown. Showing the tools score for Repairs alone, across both years, would test that claim directly.

## 4. Attribution and recommendations overreach

**The cause of any improvement can't be identified.** The 2025 programme bundled new vans, tablets, a revised bonus scheme and director-led briefings. Even if the Repairs gain were real, the survey can't show which element drove it. Recommendation 5.1 picks out briefings as "the improvement it has delivered" with no evidence for that particular element.

**The language is too strong.** The Conclusion says the Executive Team "can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked." That isn't supported. Something like "early indications are encouraging but cannot yet be confirmed, given the fall in Repairs response" would be defensible.

**A suggested reframing of 5.1:** pilot director-led briefings in one division and evaluate them, rather than rolling them out on the assumption that they work. Other evidence would help, such as Repairs turnover, sickness absence, or briefing attendance and feedback.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Overall response fell sharply.** It dropped 19 points (72% to 53%), with falls in every division. Saying it "remains above the 50% benchmark" is technically true but understates a significant decline that deserves its own investigation and a target for 2027.
- **No significance or margin of error.** Changes of 1 to 2 points (Housing Management +1, Central Services −1, Workload −2, Priorities +2) may not be meaningful. A note on which changes are statistically distinguishable would help readers.
- **"Highest since 2019" is unsupported.** Including earlier years' index values, even in a footnote, would back it up.
- **Workload is only partly analysed.** The Housing Management vacancy link rests on free-text comments. Showing workload scores by division would test it. Also clarify whether the 610 headcount includes the 41 vacant posts.
- **Recommendation 5.3 needs more.** Repeating the method unchanged risks repeating the Repairs response problem. Add an action to diagnose and fix low Repairs participation before March 2027.

## Summary of suggested changes

1. Correct 1,150 to 1,050.
2. Remove or correct "every division improved."
3. Flag the Repairs response collapse prominently and caveat the Repairs and overall gains.
4. Add divisional theme scores and a headcount-weighted index.
5. Soften the attribution claims and reframe 5.1 as a pilot with evaluation.
6. Add a recommendation to investigate and improve response rates, especially in Repairs.
